title: The Word shows different forms to different hearers
source_text: Εἰσὶ γὰρ διάφοροι οἱονεὶ τοῦ λόγου μορφαὶ, καθὼς ἑκάστῳ τῶν εἰς ἐπιστήμην ἀγομένων φαίνεται ὁ λόγος, ἀνάλογον τῇ ἕξει τοῦ εἰσαγομένου ἢ ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον προκόπτοντος ἢ ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἢ καὶ ἐγγὺς ἤδη γινομένου τῆς ἀρετῆς ἢ καὶ ἐν ἀρετῇ γεγενημένου, ὅθεν οὐχ, ὡς ὁ Κέλσος καὶ οἱ παραπλήσιοι αὐτῷ βούλονται, „μετεμορφώθη“ ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν καὶ „εἰς τὸ ὑψηλὸν ὄρος“ ἀναβὰς ἄλλην ἔδειξε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μορφὴν καὶ πολλῷ κρείττονα ἧς οἱ κάτω μένοντες καὶ μὴ δυνάμενοι αὐτῷ εἰς ὕψος ἀκολουθεῖν ἐθεώρουν, οὐ γὰρ εἶχον οἱ κάτω ὀφθαλμοὺς δυναμένους βλέπειν τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἐπὶ τὸ ἔνδοξον καὶ θειότερον μεταμόρφωσιν· ἀλλὰ μόγις αὐτὸν ἐδύναντο χωρῆσαι τοιοῦτον, ὥστε λέγεσθαι ἂν περὶ αὐτοῦ ὑπὸ τῶν μὴ δυναμένων τὸ κρεῖττον αὐτοῦ βλέπειν τό· „εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος, ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον, ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων,“ καὶ ταῦτα δὲ πρὸς τὴν Κέλσου ὑπόληψιν, μὴ νοήσαντος τὰς ὡς ἐν ἱστορίαις λεγομένας μεταβολὰς ἢ μεταμορφώσεις τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τὸ θνητὸν ἢ ἀθάνατον αὐτοῦ, λελέχθω.
pass_a_gloss: For there are differing as-it-were forms (μορφαί) of the Word, as the Word appears (φαίνεται) to each of those being led to knowledge (εἰς ἐπιστήμην ἀγομένων), proportionally (ἀνάλογον) to the state/habit (ἕξει) of the beginner (εἰσαγομένου) or one advancing (προκόπτοντος) a little or more, or already becoming near to virtue (ἀρετῆς), or having come to be in virtue. Whence not as Celsus and those like (παραπλήσιοι) him want (βούλονται) 'was transfigured (μετεμορφώθη)' our God and having gone up 'onto the high mountain (εἰς τὸ ὑψηλὸν ὄρος)' showed another form of his, much better than that which those staying below (κάτω), unable to follow him to the height (ὕψος), beheld. For those below did not have eyes able to see the Word's transfiguration (μεταμόρφωσιν) to the glorious (ἔνδοξον) and more divine; but they could scarcely (μόγις) contain (χωρῆσαι) him such, so that it might be said of him by those unable to see his better: 'we saw him, and he had no form (εἶδος) nor beauty (κάλλος), but his form dishonoured (ἄτιμον), failing (ἐκλεῖπον) beside the sons of men.' And let these be said (λελέχθω) against Celsus's assumption (ὑπόληψιν), who did not understand the changes (μεταβολάς) or transformations (μεταμορφώσεις) of Jesus spoken as in histories (ὡς ἐν ἱστορίαις), and his mortal or immortal.
pass_b_english: For there are, as it were, different forms of the Word, as the Word appears to each of those who are being led into knowledge, in proportion to the state of each: the one who is just beginning, or who has made a little progress or more, or is already drawing near to virtue, or has even come to live in virtue.

Hence, not in the way Celsus and those like him would have it, our God “was transfigured” and, going up “onto the high mountain” (Matthew 17:1-2; Mark 9:2), showed another form of himself, far better than the one seen by those who stayed below and could not follow him to the height. For those below did not have eyes able to see the transfiguration of the Word into what is glorious and more divine. They could barely receive him as he was, so that those who could not see his better form might say of him: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:2-3).

Let this be said in answer to the supposition of Celsus, who did not understand the changes or transformations of Jesus that are told in the manner of historical narrative, nor what is mortal or immortal in him.

choices.choice: 'according as' -> 'as' (archaism); listed the stages as 'the state of each: ...' for readable order
'has even come to be in virtue' -> 'has even come to live in virtue' (calque)

recast 'it is not in the sense that ... that our God was transfigured' as a parenthesis 'Hence, not in the way Celsus ... would have it, our God was transfigured' so the negation qualifies the manner, not the event
'told as in narratives of history' -> 'told in the manner of historical narrative' (stiff)

Construction: 'οὐχ, ὡς ὁ Κέλσος ... βούλονται' is taken as a parenthesis qualifying the manner ('not in the way Celsus would have it'), not as denying the event; Origen accepts the transfiguration as the Word showing a higher form to those able to see it. The parenthetical English order keeps the event outside the negation. The mountain phrase matches Matthew 17:1 / Mark 9:2 (ὄρος ὑψηλόν); μετεμορφώθη is Matthew 17:2 / Mark 9:2. Isaiah 53:2-3 is quoted from the LXX; Origen's text lacks πάντας before τοὺς υἱούς. 'εἶδος' rendered 'form' for the Isaiah quotation, distinct from μορφή, which is also 'form' in the surrounding argument; English cannot keep both apart without strain.
